title: Wearable-Triggered Spending Guardrails for Sports Bettors
angle: Finance (stablecoins, payments, embedded finance, insurance gaps, household finance) x Sports, fitness, wellness, wearables, recovery
one_liner: A debit card and betting-budget wallet that tightens gambling, day-trading and BNPL limits automatically when the wearer's sleep, heart-rate variability and late-night pattern predict impulsive decisions, with an optional spouse or sponsor as co-guardian.
customer: US adults who bet legally on sports or prediction markets and want limits: self-referred users, partners and recovery groups first. Credit unions and employer assistance programs are the B2B2C channel. The price is $6-9 a month.
problem: Roughly 40 states have legal sports betting and sports prediction contracts have spread. Household credit stress is at record levels, with delinquencies at highs and deposits often funded by cards or BNPL. Existing blocks are all-or-nothing, and willpower fails at 2 a.m. after a losing streak. A wearable knows when the user is depleted, but the bank has never seen that signal.
solution: An issued card and ledger, built on a card-issuing platform, that funds a weekly betting wallet. The user pre-commits the rules when calm. If sleep drops below a set threshold, HRV falls against baseline, or two late-night losses stack up, the wallet enters a 24-hour cooldown, cuts the daily cap, or asks a partner to approve top-ups. Wearable sync is opt-in via Oura, Whoop, Garmin or Apple Health. Only a one-bit cooldown flag leaves the phone.
why_now: Legal betting and prediction-market sports contracts scaled through 2025-26. Brazil banned online betting and announced debt relief on Sept 25, 2026, showing the politics have turned. The CFPB open-banking rule is stayed and unstable, so a business built on card-level controls avoids dependence on aggregator data. Wearables are now mainstream, with Whoop raising $575M this year.
revenue_model: $7 a month subscription plus interchange share. Credit unions and neobanks license it for $1-2 per member per month. State problem-gambling councils pay for evidence-based tools. Anything sold to sportsbooks is optional and kept separate to avoid conflicts.
non_obvious_insight: Financial products treat every hour as equal, but behavior is not. The best predictor of a regretted transaction is the user's physiological state at 1 a.m., which the user's own wearable measures and the bank never sees. Sell control, not surveillance: the user writes the rules in advance and a bank never sees raw health data.
first_30_days: Ship a no-card MVP: an SMS and Slack bot that uses the Oura or Whoop API to send cooldown alerts, plus a partner-approval flow. Recruit 50 users from recovering-bettor communities. Measure whether cooldowns cut after-midnight deposits. Then pilot with one credit union that already offers gambling merchant-category blocks, and price at $7 a month.

title: Predict Walk-In Cooler Failures Via Refrigeration Techs
one_liner: White-label predictive monitoring that local commercial-refrigeration companies sell as a maintenance plan, so a failing compressor becomes a Tuesday service visit rather than a Saturday-night emergency.
customer: Independent commercial refrigeration and HVAC-R service companies with 5-50 techs, who pay roughly $8-12 per monitored compressor per month and resell at $25-40 inside a maintenance plan. The restaurant is the end payer. A later add-on is a spoilage-insurer premium discount.
problem: A walk-in dies on Saturday at 9pm. That means an emergency call at 2-3x the rate and $8-15k of protein and dairy in the dumpster, sometimes a closed kitchen. Temperature-probe alerts only fire after the box is already warm, so they are too late. The real early signals are in the power draw: rising duty cycle from dirty condenser coils, failing fan motors and capacitors, low charge, short-cycling, and defrost heater faults. Techs spend their weekends on emergencies and have almost no recurring revenue.
solution: Clip-on current-sensing hardware (roughly $25-40 bill of materials) with a cellular or Wi-Fi gateway on each compressor and condenser fan. A model compares duty cycle and amp draw against ambient kitchen temperature and defrost cycles to flag drift weeks before the box warms. It creates a scheduled work order in the contractor's dispatch system (for example ServiceTitan) with the likely fault and parts to bring. The contractor sells it as a 'Sunday-proof plan' and gets the white-label dashboard and monthly reports.
why_now: Cellular IoT and current sensors are very cheap. Field-service software has spread through small trades, so integrations are possible. Skilled refrigeration techs are scarce and contractors need each tech to cover more boxes. The HFC phasedown (AIM Act) is changing refrigerants and service complexity, pushing repair-versus-replace decisions. Power prices are climbing, so efficiency drift now costs owners visibly.
revenue_model: Recurring B2B2B: $8-12 per monitored compressor per month to the contractor, plus hardware at cost and a per-contractor platform fee. Later, add insurer partnerships that pay for verified spoilage-loss reductions.
non_obvious_insight: The real distribution channel for restaurant equipment tech is not SaaS marketing to owners. It is 'my guy': the one refrigeration tech who answers his phone. Owners trust him, he holds the keys and the relationship, and he hates 2am calls and lacks recurring revenue. Sell to Mike, not to me. The signal is also cheaper than probes: amp draw predicts failures that temperature only reveals when it is too late.
first_30_days: Instrument 10-15 compressors and condenser fans across my two locations and five friends' restaurants with off-the-shelf clamp sensors. Log data and record every failure. Sign 2-3 local refrigeration companies as design partners with a free 60-day pilot of 50 sensors. Use the first 'caught it before Saturday' event as the case study, then sell the plan to that contractor's other accounts.

title: Closed-Loop Solvents for the Generic GLP-1 Wave
angle: Pairing 1: GLP-1 drugs x Circular economy/materials (solvent recovery)
one_liner: Solvent-recovery-as-a-service for peptide CDMOs and new generic semaglutide makers, because the pill era and the April 2026 patent expiries multiply peptide API output and its solvent waste.
customer: Generic GLP-1 manufacturers ramping in India (40+ launchers), Canada, Brazil, China and Turkey, plus peptide CDMOs and US peptide onshoring projects. The buyer is the plant's operations or EHS head, who is under margin pressure.
problem: Chemically synthesized and purified peptides are among the most solvent-hungry drugs (published process-mass-intensity estimates run around 10,000 kg of waste per kg of API, versus a few hundred for small molecules). Coupling and cleavage use DMF, NMP, DCM and TFA. RP-HPLC purification burns acetonitrile. DMF and NMP face tightening worker-exposure rules, and TFA is drawing PFAS scrutiny in Europe. Oral semaglutide needs about 25 mg a day versus 2.4 mg a week for the pen, roughly 70x more API per patient-week, so tonnage and waste balloon. Lilly's orforglipron is a small molecule and avoids this, so the burden lands on Novo's supply chain and the thin-margin generics.
solution: Containerized, GMP-adjacent recovery skids (fractional distillation, membrane polishing, carbon and ion-exchange for TFA capture) leased or run on a tolling basis. Recovered DMF and acetonitrile come back with a certificate of analysis for reuse in non-final steps, and a mass-balance ledger documents the reduced hazardous waste for regulators, auditors and customers. The first product is a paid batch-level solvent mass-balance audit, which leads to tolling.
why_now: Semaglutide patents expired across India, Canada, Brazil, China and Turkey around April 2026 and dozens of makers are scaling at once. The Wegovy pill launched Jan 5, 2026 and the pill format changes API volume by an order of magnitude or more. Solvent regulation is tightening. Acetonitrile has had repeated supply shocks.
revenue_model: Per-kg-recovered tolling fees, or a monthly skid lease plus a share of avoided virgin-solvent and incineration cost (customers typically keep 30-40% savings). Add-on fees for regulatory documentation.
non_obvious_insight: The GLP-1 story is told in doses, but its physical footprint is solvent mass. The second-tier generic makers who cannot afford incineration and cannot buy virgin acetonitrile at spot prices are the ones who will pay for recovery, not Novo or Lilly.
first_30_days: Offer five generic makers or CDMOs in Hyderabad, Ahmedabad and Ontario a free solvent mass-balance audit of one batch. Partner with an existing pharma-grade solvent tolling distiller so no capex is needed. Aim for one paid 5-10 tonne tolling pilot within 90 days and use the audit data to sell skid leases.

title: Burn-Lot Exit Desk for Fire Survivors
one_liner: Package burned lots and stranded insurance claims into sellable assets, and auction them to vetted builders at fair prices.
customer: Owners of destroyed lots in the Palisades and Altadena (free to them). Builders, small developers and community land trusts pay a success fee.
problem: About 13% of affected Palisades single-family owners have started rebuilding 18-plus months on. Insurer estimates ($462/sq ft) sit far below contractor budgets (up to $1,065). Many owners do not want to become developers, and cash buyers lowball lots.
solution: Prepare each lot as a marketable asset: claim documents (what transfers and what does not), debris and utility status, pre-approved plans and permit history. Run a competitive bid among vetted builders with three options: sell the lot, sell with claim assignment, or take a fixed-price turnkey rebuild. Handle escrow and title through partners.
why_now: Deadlines on additional-living-expense coverage and permit pipelines are biting 18 months after the fires, and the low rebuild rate shows demand for an exit.
revenue_model: A 2-3% buyer-paid success fee, builder subscriptions for deal flow, and later turnkey rebuild margin.
non_obvious_insight: 'Rebuilding services' is the obvious market. The larger one is liquidity: turning a lot plus a claim into cash at a fair price.
first_30_days: Interview 30 owners in fire-survivor groups, recruit 3 builders, and hand-run 5 lots. Use a licensed broker partner for the transaction side.

title: Harvest Inns: Motel Wings as Farm Crew Housing
one_liner: A hospitality-grade operator that master-leases wings of underused rural motels and sublets compliant beds, meals and transport to growers who cannot house H-2A crews.
customer: Fruit and vegetable growers and grower associations using H-2A labor in Georgia, Michigan, Pennsylvania, Washington and Florida. The supply side is independent rural motels and extended-stay properties.
problem: Housing is the binding constraint on legally staffing harvests. Farm crews shrank after the immigration crackdown (up to 30% of strawberry and almond crews lost in Q1 2026), grapes, blueberries and peaches rotted unpicked in 2025, and H-2A jobs are heading toward 500K. Growers do not want to run hotels, and motel owners do not want H-2A paperwork while their occupancy stays weak in a K-shaped market.
solution: Master-lease 20-40 room wings for 10-16 weeks. Run the compliance layer: DOL public-accommodation rules (50 sq ft per person, 36-inch bed spacing, cooking and laundry ratios, direct payment by the employer to housing management), pre-built state workforce agency inspection files, linens and cleaning, catered or kitchenette meals and van shuttles. Software rebooks the same crews' beds in the next county as harvest calendars move, like a hotel chain whose guests are harvest crews. Inspection-first and worker-first standards are the moat.
why_now: DOL rules explicitly allow hotels and motels as H-2A housing, with local health codes applying first. The October 2025 wage-rule change and H-2A growth mean more growers are entering a system they have never staffed. Late crews and unpicked fields are now widely reported, and lower-tier hotels are under pressure while luxury leads.
revenue_model: Growers pay roughly $22-$35 per bed-night all-in (assumption to validate), of which motels get about $12-$20. Operator margin of 20-30% plus meal and transport upsells, sold as season contracts through grower associations.
non_obvious_insight: The idle asset already exists in every farm county, and the missing party is a specialist workforce-lodging operator, the ag version of oil-field man camps, who will absorb compliance risk. Motel owners value a guaranteed off-OTA base load more than a higher rate.
first_30_days: Pick one cluster such as south Georgia blueberries and peaches or Michigan cherries. Sign 3 motels for wings of 20-40 rooms, map the state inspection process with the workforce agency, and pre-sell 2 growers before March for the spring 2027 harvest season.

title: Bring-Into-Use Satellites for Spectrum Filing Holders
one_liner: Fixed-price rideshare satellites that let holders of valuable spectrum and orbit filings meet ITU hardware milestones instead of losing them.
customer: Telecom ministries and regulators of small and mid-size states (Gulf, Africa, Pacific, Central Asia, Latin America), plus startups that hold NGSO filings but cannot afford a full constellation.
problem: Spectrum and orbit rights are now priced like beachfront (EchoStar's reported $23B sale to AT&T and $17B sale to SpaceX), yet ITU rules still require real hardware in orbit by set deadlines. A holder of paper filings is one missed milestone from losing the asset, and a real constellation costs hundreds of millions.
solution: A standard 6U-12U bus with a software-defined payload configurable to the filed bands, sold as a 'milestone in a box'. The package covers rideshare launch, operations, evidence for the administration and coordination paperwork. Regulatory counsel decides what counts as bringing into use for each filing. Entry product is a filing-health audit built from public ITU data.
why_now: The 2025-26 EchoStar deals reset what spectrum is worth. Rideshare is plentiful (321 orbital launches in 2025 per the briefing). Commercial 6U buses and SDR payloads are off the shelf, and nine-figure rounds at European bus makers show integration capacity is growing. Sovereign space programs are multiplying.
revenue_model: Audit $20-50k. Fixed-price milestone satellite $1.5-4M. Annual retainer of $100-300k for filing maintenance and coordination. Optional success fee when a preserved filing is sold or leased.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders treat filings as paper assets and hardware as optional. The ITU makes hardware the price of keeping the paper, so the scarce thing is cheap, compliant placeholder hardware plus the regulatory playbook. Nobody sells that as a product.
first_30_days: Hire one ex-administration or ITU filing specialist on contract. Scrape public ITU filing data and rank about 100 filings by deadline urgency. Send personalized audits to 50 administrations and startups, and charge for the first five. Collect LOI-backed pre-orders before committing to hardware.

title: Rent-a-Robot Creature Actors for Haunts and Events
one_liner: A rental troupe of costumed quadruped and humanoid robots, with operators and safety systems, for haunted attractions, festivals, conventions and immersive shows.
customer: Haunted attractions, seasonal theme-park events, festivals and conventions, immersive theatre producers and brand activations.
problem: Haunts struggle to hire and retain actors, and scares repeat. Fans love character robots (Disney's droids), but building one is expensive and risky, so small producers cannot offer them.
solution: Buy off-the-shelf sub-$5k quadrupeds and $6-16k humanoids and fit them with fabricated creature shells. Add a director's tablet for scripted and remote-driven behaviors, geofencing and e-stops, and insurance. Rent at $800-2,500 per night with an operator.
why_now: Cheap quadrupeds and humanoids with open-source locomotion are available, entertainment robots are already common in China, and Halloween is five weeks away.
revenue_model: Nightly rental plus operator fee, then creature shell and kit sales and character licensing.
non_obvious_insight: The hard part is not the robot, it is the show: safety envelope, character design, logistics and insurance. Amortizing hardware over 100+ nights a year makes this a creature-troupe service business, not a robotics company.
first_30_days: Lease 2 robots for about $6k and build two creature shells. Book 3-5 haunts and one convention for October and November at about $1,000 per night. Get event insurance and a written safety protocol.

title: Pre-Inspected Wildfire Books From Moratorium Zip Codes
one_liner: Turn California's public nonrenewal-moratorium ZIP lists into a supply of mitigation-verified risks, sold to carriers and MGAs who want good business and to commercial-residential owners who need it.
customer: Two payers. Admitted and E&S carriers or MGAs pay $75-150 per bound policy for a pre-inspected, standardized risk file. HOAs, apartment owners, senior-living operators and nonprofits pay $300-1,500 per building for verified defensible-space and hardening reports.
problem: California's wildfire nonrenewal moratoria last one year from the emergency declaration (up to 24 months for total losses), then the protection ends. More than 147,000 policyholders sit in 29 Gifford Fire ZIP codes, and over 64,000 in 22 Gann Fire ZIP codes. Since SB 547 took effect on 2026-01-01, commercial residential owners are covered for the first time, so they will face renewal shock too. Carriers lack standardized ground-truth mitigation evidence, and owners have no cheap way to produce it.
solution: A mitigation-verification package aligned to the state's Safer from Wildfires discount framework. It covers ember-resistant vents, Zone 0 clearance, roof class, and geotagged photo evidence with an inspector attestation. The result is a portable underwriting file. We start with commercial residential buildings, where one manager decision covers many units and the owners are reachable, and then sell the file to carriers as a pre-underwritten book.
why_now: The Gifford Fire moratorium (emergency declared 2025-12-23) expires around 2026-12-23, about 86 days from today. The Gann Fire moratorium began 2026-08-06. The FAIR Plan hit 696,562 policies and $768B of exposure in June 2026, up 157% and 250% since September 2022. Carriers have been restricting writing statewide, and the state has told them to give wildfire safety discounts.
revenue_model: Inspection fees from commercial-residential owners ($300-1,500 per building), plus per-bind fees or a basis-point share of premium from carriers and MGAs taking the verified files. Later upsell of reinspection subscriptions.
non_obvious_insight: The moratorium notices are effectively a public, geocoded list of about 210,000 policyholders whose insurability will be decided by mitigation evidence within months. See https://www.insurance.ca.gov/0400-news/0100-press-releases/2025/release002-2026.cfm (Gifford: 147,000+ policyholders, 29 ZIPs, one year from 2025-12-23, up to 24 months for total loss, SB 547 extends to businesses, associations, affordable housing, senior facilities and nonprofits) and https://www.insurance.ca.gov/0400-news/0100-press-releases/2026/release027-2026.cfm (Gann: 64,000+, 22 ZIPs). FAIR Plan growth is at https://www.cfpnet.com/key-statistics-data/. Cotality found 2.5M US properties with $1.4T wildfire exposure (https://www.cotality.com/press-releases/over-2-5m-u-s-properties-face-wildfire-risk-with-1-4tn-exposed). I could not confirm carrier re-entry commitments in this session, so the carrier-side demand is a hypothesis to test with 3 MGAs before scaling. The wedge sells to reachable commercial-residential owners first, and the carrier data sale follows once the files exist.
first_30_days: Download the ZIP lists for Gifford and Gann and geocode commercial-residential buildings (HOAs, apartments, senior living) from county parcel and permit data. Train 2 inspectors on a one-page checklist based on the state discount framework. Cold-call 40 property managers in the Gifford ZIPs before 2026-12-23 and offer a discounted first inspection. Show 3 MGAs sample files and ask what fields they would pay for.

title: Funeral Home Land-and-Business Split Advisory
angle: Pairing 2: Real estate x death/estates/wealth transfer
one_liner: An advisor that separates aging independent funeral directors' real estate from their operating business. The land goes to housing developers, the shrunken business is leased back or sold to a consolidator, and the advisor earns fees and a small equity slice.
customer: Owners of independent funeral homes (about 75% of 15,401 US funeral homes are family or privately owned), especially those over 60 without a successor. Infill housing developers and investors buy the land. Consolidators such as SCI and Everstory may buy the business.
problem: These sites were built for burial-era visitation: large buildings with big parking lots on prime corridors. With cremation at about 63%, flat deaths and volume down 1.4% at SCI, the buildings are oversized while taxes and upkeep rise. Owners get lowball offers for the business that bundle the land. Developers never see these parcels, which are off-market and not listed. The business buyer pool and the land buyer pool are disjoint and do not talk to each other.
solution: Screen parcels using zoning, lot size, transit and local cremation share, plus state licensing data on owner age. Offer owners a split: sell or ground-lease the land to a developer and lease back a compact 2,500-3,000 sf service footprint (or a ground-floor space in the new mixed-use building), or sell the business alone to a consolidator. Package parcels for states with single-staircase and missing-middle reforms. Sell paid feasibility studies first, then take closing fees and equity.
why_now: Single-staircase reform (7 states in 2025, Michigan in July 2026) and California AB 2074 lower infill costs. Rates near 7.5% make greenfield harder, so infill parcels gain appeal. Consolidator cash flow is strong (SCI operating cash flow up 43%), which makes them acquisitive. Cremation growth is making the buildings redundant.
revenue_model: $5-10K paid feasibility studies, a 2-3% success fee on the land transaction, 5-10% carried equity in the project, and a fee when the business is sold to a consolidator.
non_obvious_insight: Funeral homes are a large class of buildings whose function shrank while owners still think of them as businesses, not real estate. The highest and best use is often housing, and the key is to split the land from the operation so neither buyer pool discounts the other.
first_30_days: Pull funeral home parcels in two or three states with recent zoning reform. Contact 100 owners aged 60 or over (from state funeral-board license data). Sign three paid feasibility studies. Partner with one infill developer and one consolidator to test appetite.

title: Identical Object Kits for Robot Data Farms
one_liner: Manufacture and ship standardized kits of hundreds of everyday-object variants, panels of handles, hinges and knobs, and task fixtures, so that every home and lab collecting robot training data uses the same physical objects.
customer: Robot-learning startups and university labs, and the data-collection vendors that run gig-worker networks who record household demonstrations for humanoid and manipulation models.
problem: At-home robot data collection is booming, but contributors use whatever cups, jars and cabinet handles they own. That makes data hard to compare, hard to control for variation and impossible to replicate across sites. A robot learning to open a drawer needs the same drawer types in 500 places.
solution: A 'Kitchen-100' kit: 100 standardized, individually scanned objects (cups, lids, jars, tongs, utensils, packages), plus modular handle, hinge, latch and knob panels and drawer or door fixtures with known mass, friction and geometry. Ship to thousands of contributors and to labs. Sell new object sets monthly so datasets keep growing coherently, and bundle the digital twins (scans and physics parameters) for simulation.
why_now: Humanoid and robot-foundation-model companies are competing for training data in 2026, and coverage such as MIT Technology Review's April 2026 report on gig workers training humanoids at home shows the supply chain for that data is still improvised. Only a handful of vendors can collect at scale, and none owns the standardized physical layer.
revenue_model: Kit sales ($150 to $600 each in batches of hundreds or thousands), monthly new-object subscriptions, custom fixture builds for labs ($5k to $50k) and licensing of scan and physics data.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck for physical AI is not only more demonstrations but controlled, comparable ones. Whoever ships the same 100 objects to 5,000 kitchens gets a natural experiment in robot learning, and the kit sets the de facto benchmark. Old benchmarks (like a single reference set of household objects) are small and dated, so a manufacturing-scale, refreshable standard can become infrastructure.
first_30_days: Design and print or source a v0 kit of 50 to 100 objects and a set of handle panels. Scan each object and publish a free open dataset as marketing. Pitch 15 labs and 5 data-collection vendors with a pilot offer: 20 kits at cost plus a custom object of their choice. Target one vendor pilot of 200 kits.

title: Laid-Off Auto Technicians to Water Operators
angle: Pairing 2: Manufacturing reshoring/tariffs x Water infrastructure
one_liner: A paid-placement training pipeline that turns displaced auto and machinery technicians into licensed water and wastewater operators.
customer: Contract water operators and small utilities, paying $4-8k per placed operator. State dislocated-worker and WIOA funds cover much of the tuition.
problem: Water systems face retirements, PFAS, nitrate and 2027 lead-and-copper deadlines with too few skilled operators. Meanwhile auto OEM robot orders are down 25% and autos lost 4.5k jobs in August, while the industrial maintenance and PLC skills those workers hold are what treatment plants cannot find.
solution: An 8-12 week bootcamp that maps PLC, pump, motor and controls skills onto Grade 1-2 operator exams plus PFAS media, ion exchange and membrane basics. Each trainee has a conditional job offer as an operator-in-training before starting. Solve the experience-hours bottleneck through contract-operator trainee slots.
why_now: Auto and metals layoffs are running alongside record capital-goods orders. Compliance clocks (PFAS monitoring 2027, LCRI Nov 2027) force hiring now, and EPA money for treatment is flowing.
revenue_model: Placement fee per hire from employers, plus state workforce-fund tuition reimbursement. Optional income-share for trainees.
non_obvious_insight: The binding constraint on water treatment is not money. It is people who can keep a PLC-run plant alive, and shrinking auto plants hold exactly those people.
first_30_days: Contact state Rapid Response teams for two Midwest auto-plant layoffs. Sign one contract operator for 10 conditional offers. Run a first cohort of 12 with a community-college partner.

title: Global Rain Radar From Starlink Dishes
one_liner: Turn opted-in Starlink terminals into the densest rain-gauge network ever built and sell ground-truth rainfall to insurers.
customer: Parametric crop and flood insurers and MGAs, reinsurers, agricultural cooperatives, utilities and municipal flood teams.
problem: Rain gauges are sparse and radar coverage is poor in rural and developing regions. Parametric insurance suffers from basis risk, and disputes arise when the index does not match what happened at the field.
solution: An open-source agent reads a terminal's local signal telemetry, correlates rain-induced attenuation with rain rate, and produces minute-level hyperlocal rainfall. Owners opt in and receive a monthly credit. Sell the result as an API and as audited trigger data for parametric products.
why_now: Starlink reached 12M subscribers, including many rural users. The idea of using satellite-link attenuation as a rain sensor is established in research. Parametric insurance is growing, and public radar and gauge budgets are under pressure.
revenue_model: API subscriptions $20-200k per year per insurer or cooperative. Per-trigger data fees. Owner credits of $2-5 per month as the cost of goods.
non_obvious_insight: Rain fade is a nuisance to network engineers but a measurement to meteorologists. The sensors are already installed and paid for by their owners.
first_30_days: Adapt open-source telemetry tools and recruit 300 terminal owners with a small credit. Co-locate with 30 tipping-bucket gauges and publish a validation note. Pitch two parametric MGAs and one agricultural cooperative, and plan a fallback if SpaceX restricts local access.

title: 911 Dispatch Layer for Autonomous Fleets
angle: Pairing 2: Logistics & physical automation x Government/defense/municipal
one_liner: A RapidSOS-style shared layer inside police and fire dispatch tools that lets first responders instantly direct, reach and cite any autonomous vehicle, truck, delivery robot or drone fleet.
customer: Autonomous fleets pay per vehicle (Zoox, May Mobility, Avride, Beep, Gatik, Kodiak, Bot Auto, sidewalk-robot and drone operators). It is free to 911 centers and agencies.
problem: NHTSA sent a first-responder letter on Jul 8, 2026, and fleets rely on small remote-assistance desks (Waymo has about 70 agents on shift, with two centers in the Philippines). Every fleet has its own phone number and process, and driverless trucks have no one to talk to an inspector, since CVSA enhanced-inspection clearance lasts 24 hours and needs a trained inspector. State rules (Texas SB 2807 and California AB 1777, in effect from July 2026, verify) require emergency plans and fast compliance with geofence directives. Dispatchers have about 40 seconds and no unified tool.
solution: An add-in for dispatch systems (plus SMS and web fallback) and a fleet-side API providing geofence and closure directives with acknowledgment and a timestamped compliance receipt for the city. It also gives one-tap lookup by plate, VIN or fleet ID to a live human on that fleet's ops desk, intake and routing of 'notice of noncompliance' citations, a driverless-truck inspection scheduling module, and audit logs for regulators, with responder training cards and drills.
why_now: The state laws just took effect, fleets are multiplying (Waymo across 10-14 metros, Zoox charging fares, Tesla unsupervised in Texas and Florida, Aurora at 200 driverless trucks), and NHTSA is now actively engaging. Prior compliance tools (PrePass/Kodiak) cover only Texas and Louisiana.
revenue_model: $10-25 per vehicle per month plus a $25-60k onboarding fee per fleet, with optional municipal modules for citation processing and drills.
non_obvious_insight: The legal burden lands on fleets, but the user is a dispatcher with seconds, so you win by embedding in tools police already use and giving it away to agencies, as RapidSOS did. Fleets will pay because one standard is cheaper than hundreds of city-by-city integrations.
first_30_days: Interview 20 dispatchers and fire chiefs in Phoenix, Austin and Atlanta. Build a simple web and SMS directive-and-ack tool. Sign one mid-size fleet to a 90-day paid pilot and join the APCO/NENA standards working groups.

title: Recurring-Route Repricing Desk for Service Owners
one_liner: Read-only connect a lawn, pool, cleaning or pest route to its books, find the customers who are losing money, and hand the owner ready-to-send price-increase letters.
customer: Owners of 2-15 person recurring-service companies (lawn, pool, cleaning, pest, window) on Jobber, Housecall Pro or ServiceM8 plus QuickBooks. They pay a one-time audit fee, then a monthly retainer.
problem: Owners discover their margin problem after the fact. r/sweatystartup: "Profitable jobs on paper keep turning into break-even or worse when I look at the actual numbers after" (82/100). A Jobber Community thread is titled "Anyone else realize they were breaking even or losing money after expenses?", and its owner had a full schedule but jobs barely broke even once true payroll burden (taxes, workers comp), supplies, insurance and transaction fees were counted. Tools do not fix it: Jobber adds job costing only on its $39-199/mo plans, and Joist stops at $8/mo estimates. Fear of losing the client keeps owners from raising prices.
solution: 1) A read-only connection or CSV export of Jobber or Housecall Pro, QuickBooks or Stripe, and payroll. 2) Per-customer true margin, including labor burden, drive time, card fees and callbacks. 3) A ranked list of customers to raise by X%, re-scope or drop. 4) Auto-drafted price-increase notices, phone scripts and rebuttals for the "I'll go elsewhere" reply. 5) A churn tracker that shows what each increase cost or earned. It is sold as a productized service backed by software, not as a dashboard.
why_now: Owners are absorbing cost increases in labor, insurance and materials and cannot afford to keep pricing by feel. LLMs let a two-person team parse messy exports and receipts and allocate costs per customer, which used to take a bookkeeper hours. Incumbent field-service tools keep gating job costing behind upper tiers.
revenue_model: $149 one-time margin audit. $99-199/mo retainer for monthly re-scoring, letters and churn tracking. Optional 10% referral to insurers or payroll partners.
non_obvious_insight: Every field-service tool records revenue. The missing piece is cost allocation and the nerve to raise prices, so the paid deliverable is the letter and the script, not another dashboard. Evidence: r/sweatystartup cluster "Unprofitable Service Jobs" and "How do you price your cleaning jobs? Looking to update my rates" (https://www.ideafast.pro/pains/sweatystartup). The owner-facing forum thread is at https://community.getjobber.com/discussions/finances-forum/anyone-else-realize-they-were-breaking-even-or-losing-money-after-expenses/9694. Job costing is gated to $39-199/mo tiers and estimate tools stop at $8/mo (https://www.microgaps.com/blog/saas-niches-nobody-talking-about-2026). r/smallbusiness shows the fear: "Should I fire a client that's 50% of my revenue?" and "Client sent me a 1-star review because I charged for extra work" (https://www.ideafast.pro/pains/smallbusiness). SaaS is structurally a poor fit for tiny businesses, so a service with custom tooling wins here (https://beekeycheung.substack.com/p/saas-products-leave-small-businesses).
first_30_days: Week 1: post in r/sweatystartup and the Jobber Community offering 10 free margin audits from a CSV export. Weeks 2-3: do them by hand in a spreadsheet and record which customers each owner would raise or drop. Week 4: convert to $149 audits and pre-sell the $99/mo retainer to the first 5. Target 20 paid audits and 5 retainers within the first two months.

title: Outage Pucks: Street-Level Blackout Cover
one_liner: A $25 plug-in sensor that proves your power is out and triggers a cash payout after 12 dark hours, turning neighborhoods of pucks into their own insurance oracle and a data feed utilities will pay for.
customer: Small food businesses (corner stores, taquerias, bakeries, daycares, ghost kitchens) and households with power-dependent medical needs (home oxygen, CPAP, insulin fridges, breast-milk storage). Secondary buyers are utilities and municipal resilience programs.
problem: Outage losses (spoiled inventory, closed days, hotel stays) are small and frequent, and today they are effectively uninsurable. Utility tariffs limit liability, homeowners policies mostly ignore off-premises power failure, and no address-level proof of an outage exists, so no product can pay automatically.
solution: A cellular, battery-backed puck reports loss of mains power with tamper detection. Outages are confirmed by cross-verification when several pucks on the same feeder or block go dark together, plus utility outage feeds. Payouts are $100 at 12 hours and $100 per additional 12 hours up to $600, with a higher medical tier. The anonymized street-level outage map is sold to utilities, regulators and insurers.
why_now: Grid stress from aging distribution lines, surging data-center load and public safety power shutoffs in the West is a live concern for households and small businesses. LTE-M hardware is cheap and instant-payout rails exist. CPC/IRI's September 2026 outlooks show a very strong El Niño likely, which means an active southern storm track over California and the Gulf and Southeast this winter.
revenue_model: Puck-plus-cover subscription of $8-$12 per month, with premium share to the carrier/MGA. Data licensing to utilities and grid-resilience programs, and grant or utility-funded seats for medical-baseline customers.
non_obvious_insight: Crowd verification lets a device fleet act as a parametric oracle at a resolution utilities themselves lack on low-voltage segments, where they often learn of outages only when customers call. The insurance product pays for the sensor network, and the sensor network is the real asset.
first_30_days: Buy 200 off-the-shelf LTE-M power-loss sensors and firmware-tag them. Place them with a restaurant association and a home-health agency in one storm or shutoff-prone metro. Launch as a capped 'outage guarantee' service warranty from the company's own balance sheet while an MGA is lined up. Pitch the aggregated outage map to one utility resilience team.

title: Buyer-Side RFP Claim Verifier for Cities
one_liner: Automated reference-checking and claim-testing for the flood of AI-polished bids that city procurement offices cannot separate.
customer: Procurement offices at cities, counties, school districts and cooperative purchasing bodies with lean staff, plus state procurement agencies.
problem: Governments use GenAI to write RFPs and vendors use AI to answer them, so every response looks perfect. Dallas County is cutting IT staff. Only 5.3% of AI-related contract provisions address transparency, and local tech contracts average 7 years. A bad pick locks the city in.
solution: Ingest bids, extract every checkable claim (reference customers, uptime, certifications, incident history, prior contracts) and verify against public records, contract databases, court dockets, security advisories and automated outreach to references. Deliver a one-page evidence-scored comparison that the evaluation committee can attach to the award file.
why_now: The vendor-side tools (NationGraph raised $22.5M to help vendors read documents and write proposals) have collapsed the signal in bids. Michigan's fraud-system disaster ($20M settlement plus $78M replacement) has made buyers nervous.
revenue_model: $1.5-5K per RFP for small buyers, or annual subscription for a state or co-op ($25-100K). A per-audit fee for high-risk software and AI awards.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone is selling to the vendor who is writing. The scarce, budgeted, blame-averse buyer is the one drowning in identical documents and has no tool that raises the cost of lying.
first_30_days: Take five closed public RFPs and publish a teardown showing which claims failed verification. Offer free pre-award checks to 5 county procurement offices. Charge from the second use.

title: Peak-Window Uptime Plans for Fishing Boats
one_liner: A seasonal membership that pre-stages each boat's likely failure parts and rebuilt swap components in the harbor, provides RSW and hydraulic mechanics on call, and later adds a paid lost-peak-days cover.
customer: Bristol Bay and Prince William Sound drift and set net owners, plus seiners, who pay $2,000-4,000 per boat per season. A fleet of a few hundred boats is a $1M-plus business. Later an insurance partner underwrites the lost-time cover.
problem: Most of a boat's year is earned in about 10-14 days. With 2026's $1.72/lb, a busy boat can earn $5-15K a day at peak. Hull and machinery insurance pays for repair, never for the lost fishing days. A raw-water impeller, hydraulic hose, reel motor, fuel filter or failed RSW system takes a boat out for three days because the part is on a barge or a bush flight that's booked solid. The whole fleet breaks the same dozen components in the same ten days.
solution: Catalog the top 15-20 failure modes by engine and hydraulic setup. Stage member-funded kits in secure containers at Naknek, Dillingham, Egegik and similar harbors by June 1. Hold a rotating pool of rebuilt swap cores (injection pumps, hydraulic pumps, reel motors). Contract freelance diesel, hydraulic and RSW mechanics on retainer for guaranteed response times. Members can order from the grounds by satellite text. Phase two: verified downtime (AIS, dock check-in, mechanic log) triggers a fixed per-day payment during declared peak windows through an MGA partner.
why_now: The 2026 price rebound made every fishing day worth much more than in 2025. The fleet is aging. RSW is now paid for (about $0.15/lb bonus at some processors), yet the regional development association is funding apprentices because there aren't enough RSW technicians. Starlink lets skippers order parts and report faults from the fishing grounds.
revenue_model: Membership fees of $2-4K per boat per season, parts and swap-core margin, mechanic call-out fees, and a later per-day parametric lost-time premium shared with the underwriter.
non_obvious_insight: Downtime costs are about timing, not repair. The scarce resource at peak is the right part on the right beach within hours, and nobody sells that. It works as pooled inventory: because the fleet fails predictably, a small stockpile insures hundreds of boats. Insurance pooling for parts is cheaper and faster to launch than insurance pooling for money.
first_30_days: Interview 30 skippers and mechanics at the November Pacific Marine Expo in Seattle and by phone with Naknek and Dillingham crews. Build the failure-mode parts list by engine and hydraulic setup. Pre-sell 40 memberships with $500 deposits by February. Line up two freelance mechanics and one RSW tech. Rent a container in one harbor and stage the first 40 boats' kits by June 1.

title: Private Road Agreements That Save Rural Closings
one_liner: A flat-fee e-sign-and-record service that produces the road-maintenance and shared-well agreements lenders demand, then turns each road into a dues-collecting association.
customer: Listing and buyer agents and title/escrow officers in rural and mountain markets (CO, MT, ID, WA, OR, UT, NC/TN mountains, northern New England) pay $400-750 per transaction. Later, the households on each road pay $15-40 a month through the association.
problem: A house on a private road often has no enforceable maintenance agreement, only a handshake among neighbors. FHA, VA, USDA and most conventional underwriters want a recorded, legally enforceable agreement, and similar paper for shared wells, septics and driveways. The appraiser flags the private road and the problem lands on nobody. It surfaces 7-10 days before closing, the neighbors have no reason to cooperate, and the deal slips or dies. Between sales the road decays because nobody can collect dues.
solution: Software plus templated law. (1) Detect private vs public roads from county GIS and identify every benefiting parcel and owner. (2) Use state-specific agreement templates reviewed once by local counsel. (3) Run a multi-party e-sign, remote online notarization and e-recording workflow with a friendly neighbor-outreach script. (4) Add a lender-ready cover letter that answers the standard underwriting condition. (5) Upsell to a formal road association (entity, EIN, bank account, ACH dues billing, reserve tracking, lien rights where state statute allows) and shared well/septic agreements.
why_now: Affordability pushes buyers toward exurban and rural homes, and many of them rely on FHA, VA or USDA financing with strict access rules. Remote online notarization and e-recording are now legal and routine in most states. Counties are refusing to accept new roads into public maintenance. Wildfire-zone insurers and fire districts increasingly care about year-round road access and maintenance.
revenue_model: $495 flat per agreement package, paid by the seller through escrow or by a title partner, plus pass-through recording fees. $250 add-on per shared well, septic or easement agreement. Recurring: $29/month association software plus a payment fee on dues (about 3% + $3 per household per month). Referral fees from title partners.
non_obvious_insight: The road is not the deal-killer. The 4-30 neighbors who each have zero incentive to sign are. So the product is the neighbor-consent workflow, not the document. The other insider fact is that underwriters usually accept a simple recorded agreement signed by a majority of owners with proportional cost shares. You don't need a full HOA. Once a road has bank-account-backed dues, it becomes a sticky recurring customer that nobody else serves.
first_30_days: Pick 2 counties dense with private roads (for example the foothills of Larimer/Boulder CO, or Flathead MT). Pull active listings and cross-match them to county road-class GIS to find listings on private roads. Pay a local real-estate attorney about $2-3k to review one template. Cold-contact those listing agents with a specific message: your listing is on a private road, the lender will ask for this, and we deliver in 7 days. Sign 5 pilots at $495 and 2 title officers as referral partners.

title: Fresh-Address Desk for Medicaid Plans
one_liner: Turn Title I front offices into a consent-based channel that keeps families on Medicaid, paid per household retained by health plans and hospitals, with a revenue share to the school.
customer: Medicaid managed care plans (member retention and quality-bonus teams) and nonprofit hospitals with community-benefit budgets. Principals and PTAs are the channel partners and receive a revenue share. They do not pay.
problem: Six-month renewals and work-requirement paperwork are scheduled to hit expansion-adult Medicaid enrollees in 2027. Plans lose members when renewal mail goes to old addresses and phone numbers, and their call-center contact rates are dismal. Kids often lose coverage in the household churn even when they stay eligible. Plans cannot reach the families who most need help, and the parent hears the plan's mail as junk.
solution: A text-first, home-language 'update your info and check your renewal' flow built into the school's existing August packet and registration. A part-time parent-liaison 'benefits desk' sits in the front office a few hours a week. Data goes to a plan only with a signed opt-in parent consent, not under FERPA directory information. Plans pay a fee per verified address or phone update and per completed renewal. About 30 percent of the revenue goes to a school-controlled discretionary fund. The same desk later handles other bounty-paying programs: utility low-income enrollment, Lifeline phone and internet plans, Summer EBT, and vision and dental follow-up.
why_now: Under the 2025 budget reconciliation law, expansion-adult redeterminations move to every 6 months after the end of 2026 and work requirements begin in 2027, unless states get a delay. The post-COVID Medicaid unwinding showed that most coverage losses were procedural. Principals are also hungry for discretionary dollars after the 2025 federal freezes and cancelled school-mental-health grants.
revenue_model: Per-household bounty of roughly $25 to $75 for a verified update or completed renewal. Plans also pay an annual per-school or per-region program fee. Optional add-on bounties from utilities and phone carriers.
non_obvious_insight: The freshest address and phone database of low-income families is not held by any agency. It is held by the school secretary, who re-verifies it every August because busing, lunch and emergency cards depend on it. Families ignore the plan's letters but answer the office they trust. Principals will only say yes if the money flows back to the school and consent is explicit, and that design is the moat.
first_30_days: Pick one state and call the community-engagement or quality director at two or three Medicaid plans. Offer a 90-day pilot in 3 schools whose principals you already know, priced per verified update. Build it with Twilio and a bilingual part-timer, and use a hashed list-match to show how many of a plan's returned-mail members appear in school records. Have the principal co-sign a one-page consent form that PTA volunteers can hand out.

title: Captive Insurer for Hardened Mountain Communities
one_liner: A group cell captive where associations with verified wildfire hardening share first-loss and reinsurance capital.
customer: Condo and townhome associations and mountain-resort communities in California and Colorado with $100K-$1M master premiums, plus their management companies.
problem: Master property premiums have exploded and carriers non-renew whole associations. Reinsurers hold record capital (about $790B, secondary source), yet cannot price unknown community-level risk. Rates fell up to 25% at June 1 2026, but retail carriers pass little through.
solution: A fronted group captive with quota-share reinsurance. Each association's mitigation (IBHS criteria, ember-resistant vents, vegetation plan) is verified and modeled with forward-looking cat models now allowed by California. Members keep the first-loss layer and share the dividends. The first product is captive feasibility plus a verified-hardening scorecard at $15-30K per association, which also improves standard-market placement.
why_now: Howden says reinsurer returns could fall below cost of capital by 2027, so reinsurers want differentiated, verified books now. California's Sustainable Insurance Strategy allows forward-looking models, and Colorado now credits mitigation.
revenue_model: Feasibility fees, then management fees of 8-12% of premium plus ceded profit commission.
non_obvious_insight: The soft reinsurance window is temporary and limited by data quality. Small verified pools can lock multi-year capacity before it hardens.
first_30_days: Meet 3 management companies, score 5 associations, and talk to fronting carriers and captive managers.
